questions.q: The Court places Mendoza's vineyards within which band of elevation?
questions.exp: The Court gives Mendoza 600 to 1,200 metres (2,000 to 4,000 feet) and Salta 1,500 to 2,000 metres, the highest in Argentina. Within Mendoza, Luján de Cuyo sits at roughly 900 to 1,100 metres and the Uco Valley climbs higher still, and every hundred metres of height costs about six tenths of a degree.

questions.q: Strong sun at high altitude drives intense pigmentation in Malbec's skins. Which electric colour does the Court say the wine can show as a result?
questions.exp: The Court notes that high-grown Malbec can show an electric purple colour, because stronger sunlight and ultraviolet light push the skins to build more pigment, and the same stress thickens them. Garnet and tawny belong to older reds and wood-aged fortified wines, and ruby sits between purple youth and garnet age on the tasting grid.

questions.q: Which Argentine grape does the Court say commonly sees no oak influence at all?
questions.exp: Torrontés is made for its perfume, jasmine, rose and peach from its Muscat of Alexandria parent, so it is fermented cool in steel and bottled young without oak. Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon, by contrast, commonly see new or used barrels, French or American, as the Court's winemaking row says.

questions.q: Which white grape does the Court list beside Torrontés for Argentina, at its most taut and saline from Gualtallary in the Uco Valley?
questions.exp: Chardonnay is the second white on the Court's Argentine list and the country's leading quality white grape: saline and taut from high Gualtallary, rounder lower down, and the base of Mendoza's traditional-method sparkling wine. Where Torrontés is aromatic and unoaked, Chardonnay is often fermented or aged in French oak.

questions.q: Argentina's great house blends most often set Malbec beside which Bordeaux variety, the second red on the Court's Introductory list?
questions.exp: The Court's Introductory reds for Argentina are Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon, and the two meet in the cortes, the house blends of Mendoza, as in Cheval des Andes, a Malbec-led blend with Cabernet Sauvignon. Cabernet Franc is the rising red of the Uco Valley, bottled alone and in blends, but it is not on the Court's list.

questions.q: Bonarda and Syrah stand on the Court's Certified list of Argentine reds beside which Spanish variety?
questions.exp: Tempranillo, Spain's great red, is grown in Argentina mostly in Mendoza, long for everyday blends and now also bottled on its own. It has no tradition in the province of La Rioja, whose name misleads: that is Torrontés Riojano and Malbec country. Bonarda is Savoie's Douce Noire, and Syrah is San Juan's calling card.

questions.q: An Argentine winery has a 10,000 litre blend it wants to label as Malbec. At most, how many litres of other grapes may the blend contain?
questions.exp: The Court's Argentine rule asks 85 per cent of the named grape before a variety goes on the label, so 8,500 of the 10,000 litres must be Malbec and the other 15 per cent, 1,500 litres, may be Cabernet Sauvignon, Bonarda or any other permitted grape. Chile allows 75 per cent for wine sold at home, so the same blend there could carry more of its second grape.

questions.q: On an Argentine label, DOC stands for Denominación de Origen Controlada. In full, what does the more common tier, IG, stand for?
questions.exp: The Court's Classification row gives Argentina two quality tiers: the IG, Indicación Geográfica, a GI in English, for wine from a delimited area such as a province, a department or a soil-mapped district like Paraje Altamira, and the DOC, which adds the zone's own rules. Luján de Cuyo, recognised in 1989, and San Rafael are the DOCs a server meets.

questions.q: The Court credits immigrants from which two countries with revitalising Argentina's vineyards?
questions.exp: From 1885 the railway from Buenos Aires carried Italian and Spanish immigrants to Mendoza, and they planted for a vast home market of cheap, plentiful wine, the revival the Court's History row means. The French varieties had arrived earlier, in 1853, when Michel Aimé Pouget brought Malbec to the new agricultural school in Mendoza.

questions.q: Which herb and garlic sauce, served with steak, does the Court name as the partner for Argentine Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon?
questions.exp: Chimichurri, a sharp sauce of parsley, garlic, oregano, vinegar and oil, is served with grilled beef across Argentina, and the Court pairs steak and chimichurri with Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon. The wines' ripe fruit and firm tannin meet the fat of the meat, while the sauce's acidity and herbs lift the fruit.

questions.q: Some high-end Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon, the Court says, benefit from one particular service step before pouring. Which step?
questions.exp: A young, concentrated Mendoza Malbec or Cabernet Sauvignon opens with air, and an older one may have thrown a deposit, so the Court's service row says decanting can benefit the high-end examples. Pour slowly into the decanter over a light so any sediment stays behind in the shoulder of the bottle.
